title: Cipher and Verdict
premise: When a drowned man washes up wearing clothes stolen from her own closet, small-town coroner Tamsin Villalobos realizes the killer isn't just taunting the police—he's framing her, and he knows about the three 'accidents' she quietly unraveled years ago. The victim is connected to a fire thirty years ago that killed Tamsin's mother, a fire ruled accidental by the same coroner's office she now runs. As the statute of limitations on the original crime ticks down, Tamsin must expose a conspiracy woven through the town's founding families, including the mentor who taught her everything and the only person she's ever called family. In the end, she chooses truth over loyalty, testifying to her own quiet crimes to bring down the man who raised her, and finally claims her place in a town that never wanted her.
about_author: Coral Dunmore is the pen name of a former rural hospice nurse who spent a decade listening to the last words of small-town families before turning those confessions into fiction. She lives in a converted funeral parlor on the coast of Maine, where she writes at night and keeps bees she refuses to name.

chapters.title: The Drowned Man Wears My Coat
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A body surfaces in the millpond dressed in clothes stolen from Tamsin's own closet, down to her late mother's brooch. The police treat her as a suspect; she treats the body as a message. Emotional beat: cold dread—the invisibility she built her life on is gone.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She identifies the victim as Daniel Okafor, a returning native nobody admits expecting, and notes the drowning doesn't match the water in his lungs. Detective Reyes, new to town, notices her competence. Emotional beat: guarded professionalism masking fear of exposure.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Wore Nothing
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. The sole witness claims she saw nothing, yet describes the stolen clothes in perfect detail. Reyes suspects her; Tamsin suspects she's protecting someone. Emotional beat: the reader feels the town's loyalty is a locked room.

chapters.title: Three Accidents
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Flashback-tinged chapter revealing the three deaths Tamsin quietly solved and buried—each tied to the Harrow family. She never reported them because the evidence implicated her mentor, Coroner Ed Marsh. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing like a body in shallow water.

chapters.title: The Fire of Nineteen Ninety-Four
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She pulls the file on the fire that killed her mother, ruled accidental by Ed himself. The victim's last phone call was to the Harrow house. Emotional beat: grief sharpening into purpose as the statute's deadline appears.

chapters.title: Alibis in Amber
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. Reyes interviews the town's founding families and finds thirty-year-old alibis rehearsed word for word, still identical. Someone maintains the story. Emotional beat: creeping realization that the conspiracy is alive and tended.

chapters.title: What Ed Taught Me
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Ed Marsh, retired and beloved, offers to help with the case—and subtly warns her off the fire file. Tamsin realizes he may be protecting her or hunting her. Emotional beat: the ache of doubting the only father figure she's had.

chapters.title: The Witness Breaks Silence
chapters.summary: Witness Marisol's POV. Marisol admits she lied: she saw Daniel alive the night he died, arguing with a man whose face she won't name. She's being paid in silence—her daughter's tuition, anonymously covered. Emotional beat: terror of a mother caught between truth and survival.

chapters.title: A Fourth Death, Ruled Natural
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The town pharmacist dies of 'heart failure' hours after Tamsin requests the 1994 prescription records. Tamsin signs the death certificate with hands that shake. Emotional beat: horror at becoming complicit again by doing her job.

chapters.title: Reyes Finds the Pattern
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. Reyes maps the three old 'accidents,' the pharmacist, and Daniel Okafor onto one timeline—all witnesses or evidence-touched in the fire case. He realizes Tamsin has known longer than anyone. Emotional beat: suspicion curdling into betrayal.

chapters.title: The Closet Was Never Locked
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Someone entered Tamsin's home and took the clothes—meaning the killer has had access for years. She finds her mother's diary hidden in a false drawer, half-burned. Emotional beat: violated intimacy; the past has been in her house all along.

chapters.title: Half-Burned Pages
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The diary names a child smuggled out of the Harrow house the night of the fire—Daniel Okafor, then nine years old. He came back to claim an inheritance no one wanted exposed. Emotional beat: Tamsin's mother becomes a person again, and a target.

chapters.title: The Inheritance Clause
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. Reyes discovers the Harrow estate's trust dissolves if the fire is proven arson—meaning five living beneficiaries had motive, and the statute expires in nineteen days. Emotional beat: the clock becomes a character.

chapters.title: Marisol Runs
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol tries to flee town with her daughter and is run off the road, surviving barely. From her hospital bed she whispers a name: Ed Marsh. Emotional beat: the cost of loyalty paid in blood.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Marsh House
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin confronts Ed. He doesn't deny it; he explains he ruled the fire accidental to protect Tamsin's mother's reputation—and the town's. He claims Daniel's death wasn't his. Emotional beat: the vertigo of a mentor's love that is also a cage.

chapters.title: The Second Coroner
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. Reyes finds proof Ed falsified the pharmacist's autopsy and the 1994 report—but also that Ed was in the hospital the night Daniel died. Someone else wore his authority. Emotional beat: relief that curdles—the real killer is still hidden.

chapters.title: The Beneficiary Nobody Counts
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin realizes the trust's silent sixth beneficiary: the town itself, via the Harrow Foundation that funds the police, the clinic, Ed's pension. Everyone who lied was paid. Emotional beat: the theme lands—belonging was purchased, and she was never on the payroll.

chapters.title: Statute of Limitations
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. With three days left, the killer strikes at Tamsin directly—staging her suicide in her own office. She escapes because the staging uses her mother's brooch, and she knows she never displayed it. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into clarity; the killer's intimacy with the file is the tell.

chapters.title: The Hand That Signed
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. Reyes traces who accessed the original fire file across three decades: only Ed and his deputy, now Sheriff Anne Quist—the woman who hired Reyes and steered every interview. Emotional beat: the ground tilts; the institution itself is the suspect.

chapters.title: Verdict at the Millpond
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Quist lures Tamsin to the millpond where Daniel died, intending a second drowning in Tamsin's own clothes. Ed arrives and takes the blow meant for Tamsin, dying as he lived—interposing between Tamsin and the town's sins. Tamsin records Quist's confession. Emotional beat: grief, fury, and the terrible price of loyalty finally paid in full.

chapters.title: What I Buried, What I Kept
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin testifies to the three deaths she concealed, surrendering her license, and gives the court the full arson case before the statute expires. Quist is arrested; the Foundation dissolves. Emotional beat: costly honesty—the truth costs her everything she built to hide behind.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name, Including Mine
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, months later. Working as a records clerk, Tamsin re-buries her mother under a corrected death certificate and finds the town, unpurchased for the first time, awkwardly offering her a place in it. Marisol's daughter delivers flowers. Emotional beat: belonging earned, not inherited—quiet, imperfect, real.
